mcqs.question: A 100MB contiguous file needs 25,600 individual block pointers under classic indexed allocation. How does an extent-based scheme represent the same file more efficiently?
options: It compresses the file's actual content before storing it
It stores the file only in RAM, never persisting block locations to disk
It splits the file into 1024 equal pieces regardless of actual layout
It stores one compact record — a starting block and a length — covering the entire contiguous run instead of one pointer per block
mcqs.explanation: An extent describes a contiguous run as (start, length), collapsing what would be thousands of individual pointers into one record when the blocks are actually adjacent. This is a metadata efficiency gain, not compression, and has nothing to do with RAM-only storage or a fixed split count.

mcqs.question: In a copy-on-write file system, what happens when you modify an existing block of a file?
options: The old block is overwritten immediately, exactly like a traditional file system
The new version is written to a newly allocated block, and metadata is atomically repointed to it; the old block stays until nothing references it
The modification is rejected — CoW file systems only support appending, never modifying
Both the old and new blocks are merged into one larger block
mcqs.explanation: CoW never overwrites in place — it writes elsewhere and repoints. The old block survives, unreferenced-yet, until it's safe to reclaim (or until a snapshot stops referencing it), which is the mechanism behind both crash safety and cheap snapshots.

mcqs.question: Why can ZFS snapshots be nearly instant regardless of file size?
options: ZFS silently limits snapshots to files smaller than 1GB
A snapshot compresses the entire dataset in the background before completing
Taking a snapshot only saves the current root pointer of the block tree — no data is copied, since CoW means old blocks already remain untouched until overwritten
Snapshots are pre-computed continuously in the background, so the visible operation is just a label change
mcqs.explanation: Because CoW never overwrites data in place, the old version of every block is already sitting on disk, untouched, whenever a new version is written. A snapshot just remembers the pointer to the current tree — a metadata operation, not a data copy — which is why it completes in milliseconds regardless of dataset size.

mcqs.question: A disk's own error correction fails to catch a subtly corrupted sector, and a traditional ext4 file system reads it. What happens?
options: ext4 automatically detects and repairs it from a backup copy
The read fails with an I/O error every time
ext4 refuses to mount until the corruption is manually fixed
The corrupted bytes are simply read and used — ext4 has no mechanism to detect silent corruption the disk itself doesn't report
mcqs.explanation: Without end-to-end checksums, a traditional file system trusts whatever the disk hands back. If the disk itself doesn't flag an error (bit rot), the corrupted data is silently used — no automatic detection or repair. This is exactly the gap ZFS/Btrfs checksumming closes.

mcqs.question: A team needs frequent point-in-time snapshots of a database volume plus protection against silent disk corruption. Which file system property matters most for this requirement?
options: Contiguous allocation for maximum sequential throughput
A larger journal size on ext4
Using FAT32 for maximum compatibility
Copy-on-write with native checksumming, as in ZFS or Btrfs
mcqs.explanation: Cheap, frequent snapshots and corruption detection are specifically what CoW file systems with checksumming provide natively. ext4's journal only protects metadata structure, not data corruption detection, and neither contiguous allocation nor FAT32 addresses either requirement.

mcqs.question: What's a genuine downside of copy-on-write file systems like ZFS or Btrfs compared to a traditional in-place file system like ext4?
options: They cannot detect data corruption at all
Files modified in small random chunks over time (databases, VM disks) can progressively fragment, since each change writes to a new location instead of overwriting in place
They cannot support more than one file per directory
They require manual journaling to be enabled separately
mcqs.explanation: CoW's never-overwrite model is exactly what causes fragmentation under small random writes — each change relocates rather than reuses. CoW file systems are actually stronger at corruption detection (the opposite of the first option), have no such per-directory limit, and don't need separate journaling since consistency comes from the CoW design itself.
